kind: destination_tours

buttonLabel: "Learn more about tours through Calama"
lead: >-
  Calama is an important transport hub in northern Chile. Many Ada Tours itineraries pass through El Loa Airport on their way to San Pedro de Atacama, Moon Valley, high-altitude lagoons, and geysers. Some continue from the Atacama to Patagonia; others cross the Bolivian plateau toward Uyuni and Peru. Compare the itineraries and find out how a connection in Calama differs from a city sightseeing excursion.
---

## Why Calama appears on Chile itineraries

[Calama](/chile/place/calama/) most often serves as an arrival or departure point for visits to [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/). It is convenient to fly from Santiago to El Loa Airport and then continue by car into the desert region of salt flats, volcanoes, and high-altitude lagoons. As a result, a tour program may show "Santiago – Calama – San Pedro," although nature sightseeing begins outside Calama itself.

According to Chile's official tourism portal, the drive from Calama airport to San Pedro takes approximately one hour. Actual travel time depends on the route and transfer arrangements. When choosing a tour, check the order of flights and road transfers rather than treating Calama as a standalone day of city sightseeing.

Calama also matters on multi-country journeys: after the Atacama, an itinerary may cross the high-altitude border region toward Bolivia's lagoons and Uyuni Salt Flat. The specific border crossings and overnight locations depend on the chosen program.

## Which tours through Calama should you choose?

For travelers who want to explore **Chile only**, itineraries combining the Atacama and southern Patagonia are suitable. The [seven-day Santiago, Atacama and Torres del Paine tour](/chile/tour/chile-santiago-atacama-torres-del-paine/) uses Calama as the arrival point before Moon Valley, lagoons, and geysers. The itinerary then moves on to the landscapes of Torres del Paine.

The [12-day tour including Easter Island](/chile/tour/best-of-chile-easter-island-12-days/) features a similar northern section but adds Patagonia and Rapa Nui. This suits travelers prepared for several flights in exchange for variety: desert, granite mountains, and Polynesian cultural heritage cannot be experienced within one small area.

For a trip linking **three countries**, consider [Chile, Bolivia and Peru in 12 Days](/multi-country/tour/chile-bolivia-peru-group-12-days/). Here Calama connects Santiago with San Pedro, after which the journey continues to Uyuni, La Paz, Cusco, and Machu Picchu. Calama provides access to the high-altitude portion, but most time is devoted to other sights.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_chili_santyago_pustynya_atakama_torres_del_pajne,tour_source_chili_samoe_luchshee,tour_chile_bolivia_peru_group_12_days_2026,tour_bolivia_chile_hidden_treasures_16_days}}

## The Atacama after Calama: what is actually visited?

Individual excursions differ between short and long itineraries. On the [seven-day Chile tour](/chile/tour/chile-santiago-atacama-torres-del-paine/), arriving in Calama is followed by a transfer to San Pedro and a visit to [Moon Valley](/chile/place/moon-valley-atacama/). Later stages list high-altitude lagoons, the Atacama Salt Flat, and the Tatio geysers.

The [Chile–Bolivia–Peru group program](/multi-country/tour/chile-bolivia-peru-group-12-days/) also uses San Pedro to prepare for the onward high-altitude journey. An evening astronomy excursion is offered there as an optional activity, so it must not automatically be included in the base price.

If your priorities are the night sky, lagoons, or long stops for photography, compare the actual number of nights in San Pedro. Landing in Calama does not guarantee that an itinerary includes the geysers, every lagoon, and an astronomy program. Each trip has its own daily schedule.

## Calama and Uyuni: high-altitude logistics

On multi-country itineraries from Chile to Bolivia, the order of altitude gain and organization of the overland crossing matter more than the direct distance from Calama. Desert-side San Pedro is lower than many parts of the Altiplano, and later excursions take place at high elevation. Travelers need a sensible pace, sun protection, water, and attention to how they feel.

The separate [16-day Hidden Treasures of Bolivia and Chile tour](/multi-country/tour/bolivia-chile-hidden-treasures-16-days/) travels in the opposite sequence: from Bolivia and Uyuni via San Pedro and Calama to Santiago, then onward to Patagonia and wine regions. Calama's appearance on both itineraries therefore does not imply the same border crossing, number of flights, or physical demands.

When choosing a combined journey, Ada Tours helps compare the country order, connection times, and acclimatization needs. Specific border and visa rules depend on citizenship and travel dates; there is no single rule for everyone.

## Planning the flight and transfer day

Check your arrival airport, whether the required transfer to San Pedro is included, when the first excursion begins, and how much free time remains after landing. Daytime and nighttime temperatures differ sharply in the Atacama, so layered clothing is best; take water, sun protection, and closed-toe footwear for walks.

If arrival and a sunset excursion are scheduled on the same day, the flight connection is crucial: a delay can shorten the activity. If high-altitude lagoons or geysers are planned the following day, consider your physical readiness in advance. For other destinations as well as tours, browse the [Chile tours catalog](/chile/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about Calama tours

### Do I have to stay overnight in Calama?

Not necessarily. Several Ada Tours itineraries include a direct transfer to San Pedro de Atacama after landing. Overnight arrangements depend on the chosen tour.

### Are Calama and San Pedro de Atacama the same place?

No. Calama is a separate city with El Loa Airport, while [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) is the base for excursions into the desert and surrounding landscapes.

### Can I travel from Calama toward Uyuni?

On some multi-country programs, yes, via San Pedro and the high-altitude border with Bolivia. Confirm the route, transport, and entry requirements for your tour.

### Do all tours passing through Calama include the Tatio geysers?

No. Read the specific itinerary. Flying into Calama provides a transport connection to the Atacama but does not by itself confirm visits to geysers, lagoons, or optional excursions.

## Caleta Tortel: a village of wooden walkways beside Patagonian fjords

Caleta Tortel is a coastal settlement in southern Chile's Aysén Region, near the mouth of the Baker River. Its defining feature is immediately apparent: houses stand on steep, forested slopes above the water, and an extensive network of wooden boardwalks, stairs, and pedestrian connections replaces ordinary town streets.

Visitors come to explore the village itself. Wooden walkways lead to piers, viewpoints, and homes, revealing fresh views of water, forest, and mountains at every turn. Caleta Tortel is a fascinating stop on a Carretera Austral road trip or potentially on an expedition cruise through Chilean fjords.

## Why are there wooden walkways instead of streets?

The settlement developed in difficult terrain: steep slopes, a rocky shore, wet soil, and heavy rainfall made conventional roads hard to build. Residents connected their homes and docks with wooden passages, which gradually developed into an extensive pedestrian network.

An historically important material was **Guaitecas cypress** (*ciprés de las Guaitecas*), whose wood withstands the damp climate. Its use is linked to the region's forestry history and former timber operations. The species is now protected, so the walkways represent not only construction techniques but also memories of the village's economic past.

Chile's National Monuments Council designated Caleta Tortel's historic area a **Zona Típica (Typical Zone) in 2001**. The protection covers not a single outstanding building but the combination of houses, piers, boardwalks, slopes, and vegetation that gives the place its distinctive character.

## What to see on a walk

### Boardwalks, stairways, and piers

The main route follows wooden paths along the water and between residential areas. Small viewing platforms, stairways, and branches toward piers appear at different points. Take your time: the route climbs and descends slopes, and surfaces can become slippery after rain.

Remember that Caleta Tortel is still a working residential community. Residents use the boardwalks for daily life, and boats may be operating at the piers. This is a chance to see how a real Patagonian coastal village functions while respecting private homes and work areas.

### Views of the water, forest, and Baker River mouth

The village stands near the meeting of the Baker River and southern sea channels. Forested mountains rise close to the shore, and changes in light and cloud cover dramatically alter the landscape. After rain, the wood darkens and wet greenery makes the hillsides look especially rich.

For an overview, climb to one of the accessible viewpoints. From above, it is easier to see how paths connect clusters of houses and why a conventional grid of straight streets would be poorly suited to the terrain.

## Caleta Tortel on Chilean Patagonia itineraries

On a trip along the **Carretera Austral** (Route 7), Caleta Tortel is a detour offering an insight into life in southern Patagonia. The road reaches the settlement area, but its historic center is explored mainly on foot. A longer visit requires allowing for its remote location, weather, and the return drive.

Another option is a marine expedition through the fjords. On our current [Patagonia and Chilean Fjords tour](/multi-country/tour/patagonia-chilean-fjords/), a visit to Caleta Tortel is **planned if weather permits** at one stage of the journey. The ship then continues through Messier Channel and toward the southern glacier region. This differs from an independent road trip: stop duration and the decision to land depend on the ship's schedule.

The surroundings of Caleta Tortel form part of the wider geography of the Patagonian fjords. Cruise itineraries also visit [Bernardo O'Higgins National Park](/chile/place/bernardo-ohiggins-national-park/) and [Laguna San Rafael National Park](/chile/place/laguna-san-rafael-national-park/). Those offer different experiences: glaciers and waterways, while Caleta Tortel itself is chiefly about architecture and coastal community life.

## How much time to allow and when to come

Even a short visit should allow time for the boardwalks, waterfront stops, and stairway climbs. Rushing through the village leaves little opportunity to understand its layout. For a relaxed visit or a trip with children, consider changes in elevation and slippery surfaces.

Southern Aysén has a wet climate, and rain and wind are possible throughout the year. Long summer daylight hours help with planning, but **good weather is never guaranteed**. A waterproof jacket, shoes with good grip, and a small backpack that leaves your hands free for handrails are useful.

If Caleta Tortel forms part of a longer itinerary, compare the time needed for the walk with road-transfer or ship schedules. Given its remoteness, leave time in reserve and agree the order of stops beforehand.

## How Caleta Tortel differs from other Patagonia destinations

Large nature parks are mainly associated with glaciers, lakes, and trekking. Caleta Tortel reveals something else about the region: **how people adapted a settlement to forested slopes and a marine coastline**. Even without a long hike, the connection between terrain, local materials, and architecture is apparent.

It works well as a stop on a cruise or Carretera Austral journey, but it does not replace a day in a glacier park. Each place reveals a different side of Patagonia.

## Frequently asked questions about Caleta Tortel

### Is it true that Caleta Tortel has no conventional streets?

The historic area is connected by wooden walkways and stairways rather than an ordinary street grid. You can drive to the settlement, but explore its coastal neighborhoods on foot.

### Why are the paths made of wood?

Boardwalks helped connect homes and piers across steep, wet slopes. Local timber, including Guaitecas cypress, was used historically.

### Can Caleta Tortel be visited on a cruise?

Yes, it appears on expedition routes through Chile's fjords. On the [Ada Tours itinerary](/multi-country/tour/patagonia-chilean-fjords/), the stop depends on weather and landing conditions.

### When is it best to walk the wooden paths?

In daylight and suitable footwear. Rain is possible year-round, so non-slip shoes and waterproof clothing are useful in any season.

### Is it worth visiting separately from the glaciers?

Yes, if you are interested in the architecture and life of a small Patagonian village and walking by the water. For grand glacier panoramas, add the relevant national park to your itinerary.

## Which tour visits Caleta Tortel?

[Caleta Tortel](/chile/place/caleta-tortel/) is included in the [nine-day Patagonia and Chilean Fjords expedition cruise](/multi-country/tour/patagonia-chilean-fjords/). The vessel travels along Chile's coast from the Puerto Montt area toward Tierra del Fuego and Argentina's Ushuaia. Day five of the program is titled "Caleta Tortel and Messier Channel."

A visit to Caleta Tortel or its immediate surroundings is planned **weather permitting**. This is a crucial qualification: the possibility of going ashore depends on navigation conditions. After the intended stop, the ship continues through Messier Channel and the narrow sections of southern Patagonia's waterways.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_patagoniya_i_chilijskie_fordy}}

## Why Caleta Tortel differs from other Patagonia stops

The village's distinguishing feature is its network of wooden boardwalks, stairs, and bridges connecting waterfront houses with the hillside. It lies in the Aysén Region, near the Baker River mouth. Chile's tourism portal describes it as a place where wooden pedestrian passages replace conventional streets.

The appeal is not a single monumental attraction but the village's layout: houses beside the bay and on the slopes, wooden walkways, damp forest, and water views. Unlike the glacier fronts on subsequent cruise days, it offers a stop where physical geography and residents' everyday life are visible together.

To photograph the village from the water and walk its boardwalks, suitable landing weather and adequate time are needed. The cruise does not promise a full walking circuit of every path; confirm the stop's duration for your chosen sailing.

## Where Caleta Tortel fits into the ship's route

Before Tortel, the cruise passes Puerto Montt, Aysén's island channels, glacial areas around San Rafael, and the Gulf of Peñas. The village appears at the next stage, followed by Messier Channel and the narrow passage known as Angostura Inglesa. This is a sea passage through a fjord system, not a road circuit among regional villages.

After Tortel comes [Bernardo O'Higgins National Park](/chile/place/bernardo-ohiggins-national-park/), with planned Zodiac approaches to Amalia Glacier or another glacier along Peel Fjord. These two neighboring days offer a contrast: wooden houses and the coastal life of Aysén, followed by ice walls and mountain slopes.

The ship then continues to the Strait of Magellan, Tierra del Fuego, and Ushuaia. Sailings in the opposite direction may follow a different sequence; verify the actual dates and ports before booking.

## Cruise or independent road visit

Caleta Tortel is accessible by land as well as sea. It is familiar to travelers on the Carretera Austral, the road through Chilean Patagonia. But a road trip is a different experience: it allows more time for walking and the surroundings, whereas a cruise fits a short shore visit into a longer maritime journey.

The expedition cruise has the advantage of exploring otherwise difficult-to-reach coastline without constant road transfers. The trade-off is that landing depends on weather and crew decisions. If Caleta Tortel is your main goal, consider adding a dedicated land-based stage rather than building the whole trip around one conditional landing.

## Preparing for a boardwalk visit

Wooden surfaces can be slippery after rain, and some sections have stairs and uphill climbs. For a landing, bring shoes with good grip, a waterproof jacket, and a way to protect your camera or phone from spray. Check in advance whether the visit involves transfer to a small boat, a walking section, and a return to the ship within a specified time.

Pack for the following glacier stages as well: conditions beside the water can be cool even on sunny days. The full equipment list depends on the season and vessel, so compare it with the actual itinerary.

## When to choose a cruise featuring this stop

For travel through Chile's fjords, the important factors are the individual vessel's sailing season and the coherence of the full itinerary. Listing Tortel does not guarantee a landing. For travelers mainly interested in glaciers and seascapes, the voyage remains worthwhile even if one outing changes, but the possibility is worth discussing beforehand.

Before booking, confirm with us the direction of sailing, starting and ending ports, Chile–Argentina border rules, available small-boat excursions, and physical mobility requirements. Other maritime formats can be compared in [Cruises and Expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours through Caleta Tortel

### Can you see the village's wooden walkways on the cruise?

Yes, a visit to Caleta Tortel or its surroundings is planned. However, going ashore depends on weather and the ship's approach conditions.

### Are Caleta Tortel and Bernardo O'Higgins Park visited on the same day?

No. On the [Chilean fjords cruise](/multi-country/tour/patagonia-chilean-fjords/), Tortel and Messier Channel form one stage, while the glaciers of Bernardo O'Higgins Park feature on the following stage.

### Can you reach Caleta Tortel by land?

Yes. The village lies in the Aysén Region and can be reached via Patagonia's road network. That requires separate land transport and differs from a conditional cruise landing.

### What matters most when choosing a date?

The actual sailing direction, planned landing, seasonal weather restrictions, and time ashore. These factors determine whether the village can be explored at a relaxed pace.

lead: >-
  Cape Horn, in the far south of Chile, is a famous maritime landmark near the entrance to Drake Passage. It is visited on expedition cruises through Tierra del Fuego and on some itineraries toward Antarctica. What matters here is not walking distance but weather, sea conditions, and whether landing on the island is possible. Discover the difference between sailing past the cape and walking to its lighthouse, and how to choose a sea itinerary.
---

## Cape Horn: where is Tierra del Fuego's legendary southern landmark?

Cape Horn, or Cabo de Hornos, lies on Hornos Island (Isla Hornos) at the southern end of Chile's Tierra del Fuego archipelago. The open waters of Drake Passage stretch south of the island. This is the setting for countless stories of long voyages between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

It is **an island headland of the archipelago**, not a mainland viewpoint accessible by road. Reaching the cape therefore requires travel by sea. Even if a ship sails near Cape Horn, however, that does not necessarily mean its passengers can land on the island.

## Why Cape Horn is famous among sailors

Before the development of shorter shipping routes, vessels connecting the Atlantic and Pacific rounded the southern tip of South America. The region became notorious for strong westerly winds, enormous waves, and difficult weather. Sheltered shores are scarce, and the seas south of the archipelago are exposed to ocean currents and winds.

Cape Horn's history is also tied to 17th-century Dutch navigators, who described the route around Tierra del Fuego. Its name later became a symbol of a challenging ocean passage. Today passenger cruises allow visitors to see this area without taking part in an actual sailing voyage, but weather still controls what ships can do.

## Landing on the island: lighthouse, memorial, and walk

Hornos Island has a lighthouse and an albatross-shaped memorial to sailors who crossed these waters. If the vessel can approach safely and the crew organizes a landing, passengers travel ashore in small expedition boats. A developed trail and wooden boardwalks lead to the memorial sites.

**Safe approach from the sea is the key requirement.** Wind, waves, and visibility may prevent a landing even after the ship reaches the cape. Cruise descriptions should therefore distinguish three possibilities:

| Format | What it means |
|---|---|
| Sailing past the cape | Viewing from aboard |
| Approaching the island | An attempt to reach the shore |
| Landing | Going ashore in suitable weather |

Seeing the island from the ship and walking on it are different experiences. A weather-related landing cancellation does not mean that the ship failed to reach Cape Horn.

## How to get to Cape Horn

For visitors to the far south, common starting points include [Punta Arenas](/chile/place/punta-arenas/), [Puerto Williams](/chile/place/puerto-williams/), and [Ushuaia in Argentina](/argentina/place/ushuaia/). There is no road to Hornos Island; the onward route depends on the particular ship, departure port, and sequence of stops.

Expeditions through Chile's fjords and Tierra del Fuego channels differ from longer cruises to Antarctica. On the former, Cape Horn may be a highlight of a voyage between Patagonian ports. On the latter, it may come before crossing Drake Passage toward Antarctic waters. Embarkation and disembarkation ports cannot be inferred from the name "Cape Horn" alone.

For example, our [Tierra del Fuego Fjords tour](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/) includes a five-day passage through the archipelago's straits and bays with a stage near Cape Horn. Our [Antarctica and Patagonia Express tour](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/) includes an approach to the cape during the maritime leg before Drake Passage, with a possible landing if conditions are favorable. They are different products, and their respective terms should be read separately.

## When to travel and how to prepare for the weather

Expedition cruises around the far south of South America generally operate in the warmer part of the Southern Hemisphere year, but approaching the island depends on the actual day's weather. Even in summer, conditions can be cold, windy, and wet. Sea journeys require flexibility: the crew may change the order of visits or skip a landing because of the sea state.

Bring waterproof and windproof layers, non-slip shoes, a hat, and moisture protection for photographic equipment. For small-boat landings, crew instructions are especially important: boarding procedures, life jackets, and the physical demands depend on the individual vessel.

Passengers prone to seasickness should consider rough seas and discuss preventive measures with a doctor in advance. Sailing in sheltered channels and entering the open waters of Drake Passage can feel very different.

## Cape Horn's nature and biosphere reserve

The archipelago belongs to the subantarctic natural zone. Low vegetation, wet coastal landscapes, marine ecosystems, and habitats for seabirds occur here. Sightings of particular species depend on season and weather; proximity to the island never guarantees an encounter.

A large part of Chile's far south is included in the **Cabo de Hornos Biosphere Reserve**, recognized by UNESCO in 2005. It encompasses extensive terrestrial and marine ecosystems, not just the cape itself. UNESCO biosphere reserves and UNESCO World Heritage sites are distinct designations and programs.

To complement a sea expedition with land routes, consider [Torres del Paine and Puerto Natales](/chile/place/puerto-natales-torres-del-paine/) or other [cruises and expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/). These offer different landscapes and preparation requirements, so allow for travel between regions.

## Choosing a cruise that visits Cape Horn

Begin with the main question: is it most important to see **Cape Horn itself**, spend several days among fjords, or reach Antarctica? Then compare embarkation port, voyage duration, number of days at sea, and landing conditions. Sharing the name of a geographic destination does not make two routes equivalent in experience.

In the [multi-country travel catalog](/multi-country/) and [Chile tours](/chile/tour/), check the exact order of stops. If Cape Horn is listed, establish whether the ship will merely sail past or attempt a landing. Every shore activity in this area remains weather-dependent.

## Frequently asked questions about Cape Horn

### Can I drive to Cape Horn?

No. The cape is on Hornos Island, and reaching it requires a sea voyage. Roads from southern towns do not extend to the cape.

### Do cruises always land passengers on Hornos Island?

No. Landings depend on wind, sea conditions, and decisions by the captain and crew. Some routes include only sailing near the cape.

### Is Cape Horn in Antarctica?

No. It is part of Chile, at the southern end of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago. Antarctica is farther south, across Drake Passage.

### When is the best time for an expedition?

Choose among the available expedition sailings, generally in the warmer months of the Southern Hemisphere. Favorable weather is not guaranteed in any month; landing conditions are assessed on site.

## Tours with a possible landing at Cape Horn

[Cape Horn](/chile/place/cape-horn/) is on Hornos Island in the southern Tierra del Fuego archipelago. The open waters near its cliffs are closely tied to the history of long-distance sea voyages between the Atlantic and Pacific. Expedition vessels now approach the cape, but landing on the island depends on weather, waves, and crew instructions.

Here the phrase "can visit" has a special meaning. This is **not a standalone excursion that can always be purchased as an extra**, but a conditional part of a sea route: the captain judges whether approach and landing are safe. Even when the ship passes Cape Horn, passengers may not be able to step ashore.

## Which tour includes an approach to the cape?

[Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, and Patagonia in 18 Days](/multi-country/tour/argentina-chile-bolivia-cruise-tour-18-days/) combines three countries with an expedition cruise through Tierra del Fuego's fjords. It covers the Atacama, Uyuni, Torres del Paine, Punta Arenas, then southern Patagonia's maritime section and Ushuaia.

The Cape Horn cruise day follows other sections of the southern channels. The ship travels along Murray Channel between Navarino and Hoste islands, then heads toward the cape. A landing on Hornos Island may be possible in favorable weather. If conditions are unsafe, the itinerary continues according to the captain's decision.

| Stage | Condition |
|---|---|
| Approaching the cape by sea | Part of the cruise itinerary |
| Landing on the island | Only when weather is safe |
| Walking ashore | If the crew authorizes a landing |

This distinction is essential for planning. Our tour includes the sea route past Cape Horn and a possible landing, but does not guarantee that every passenger will set foot ashore. Approaching the continent's southern extremity remains a memorable experience even if the ship cannot land.

## What is on Hornos Island?

Cape Horn is within Cabo de Hornos National Park. The island has a lighthouse and an albatross-shaped memorial commemorating sailors who crossed the dangerous southern seas. Chile's official tourism portal describes a route to these sites using wooden boardwalks and steps when an expedition landing is permitted.

The landscape is open, windy, and rugged: low vegetation, rocky shores, cold sea, and fast-changing clouds. This is quite different from walking through Patagonia's forests or visiting glacial bays within sheltered channels.

Landing from small expedition boats requires compliance with crew instructions. Warm waterproof clothes, shoes with good grip, and protection for personal belongings matter even on a brief shore visit. Wind can make the air feel significantly colder.

## How Cape Horn differs from an Antarctic cruise

Cape Horn is a geographic landmark at Chile's southern edge. Antarctica is farther south across Drake Passage. A voyage past the cape may form part of a Tierra del Fuego fjords cruise **without entering Antarctica**. Other expeditions combine the approach with a crossing into Antarctic waters.

When choosing, check the actual geography confirmed in the itinerary. The [18-day Argentina, Chile, and Bolivia tour](/multi-country/tour/argentina-chile-bolivia-cruise-tour-18-days/) is chiefly about South America and its fjords. If your goal is to land on the Antarctic Peninsula or the South Shetland Islands, choose from [Antarctic expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/) and check their own itineraries and dates.

A further comparison for maritime stages is the [Tierra del Fuego Fjords tour](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/), where the southern straits and islands are the main focus of the journey.

## When to plan the maritime section

Cape Horn's climate is shaped by the ocean and strong winds. Calm seas cannot be promised for any specific date; even in a favorable season, expedition landings can be restricted. It is wiser to choose an itinerary for its overall coverage of the fjords than to base expectations on one supposedly guaranteed island landing.

If stepping ashore is particularly important to you, discuss that priority before choosing a cruise. The organizer can confirm whether a landing attempt is planned, but the actual decision remains the captain's.

## Frequently asked questions about Cape Horn visits

### Is passing Cape Horn the same as landing on the island?

No. A ship can sail past the cape without landing guests. Going ashore depends on weather and sea conditions.

### Is Cape Horn included in the 18-day tour?

Yes. The maritime section of the [18-day journey](/multi-country/tour/argentina-chile-bolivia-cruise-tour-18-days/) includes an approach to the cape and a possible landing in favorable conditions.

### Is Cape Horn in Antarctica?

No. It belongs to Chile, in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago. Expedition ships must travel farther across Drake Passage to reach Antarctica.

### What should I pack for a short landing?

Warm waterproof clothing, shoes with reliable grip, and protection for your camera. The cruise operator determines the specific requirements.
